children: Copper prices in London softened on Monday, weighed down by a buildup in warehouse stocks that eased supply worries and on concerns about high energy prices.
on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.56% at $14,242.5 a metric ton by 0300 GMT.
The most-traded copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange
rose 0.55% to 108,720 yuan ($16,299.36) a ton, tracking Friday's overnight LME gains.
Copper stocks in LME warehouses (MCUSTX-TOTAL) surged last week to their highest levels since July, after a batch of deposits into LME-registered warehouses, mostly located in North America.

Expectations of a potential tariff on imports of refined copper into the US have pulled the metal into the country, thinning stocks elsewhere and pushing the metal on the LME to a record high of $14,875 a ton on September 11.
Macro fears and expectations of a shift in the draw of metal into the US are contributing to a bearish backdrop on copper, Alastair Munro, senior metals strategist at Marex, said in a note.
Meanwhile, oil prices started the week lower, but remained at elevated levels after a spree of attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis raised geopolitical risks.
Higher energy costs dampen global economic sentiment and have weighed on demand expectations for growth-dependent copper, which is used in electrification, construction, and consumer goods.
Providing some support, the Yangshan copper premium (SMM-CUYP-CN), a gauge of China's appetite for imported copper, was at $168 a ton on Friday, its highest since 2014.
In China, the world's biggest copper consumer, some smelters are in maintenance, with stocks in SHFE-monitored warehouses (CU-STX-SGH) falling more than a quarter to 54,356 tons last week.
